strengths: Addresses an important, timely, and underexplored safety and robustness issue in visual document reasoning: the susceptibility of MLLMs to misleading data visualizations.
Comprehensive experimental setup in Experiment 1 evaluating 18 modern MLLMs spanning proprietary, open-weight generalist, and chart-specialized models across multiple scales.
Detailed analysis distinguishing between parametric knowledge reliance vs. visual interpretation, and comparing human vs. MLLM failure modes across different misleader types.

Proposes and empirically assesses six concrete inference-time mitigation techniques, including table-based QA and chart redrawing, and transparently analyzes trade-offs such as degradation on non-misleading charts and reliance on intermediate table extraction quality.
weaknesses: The dataset size is relatively small (n = 143 misleading charts across 17 categories, and n = 124 non-misleading charts). Many misleader categories have very few samples (e.g., n = 1 for missing data, overplotting, and inappropriate pie chart; n = 3 for concealed uncertainty and missing normalization), making fine-grained per-category conclusions statistically tenuous.
Experiment 2 (consistency evaluation) is based on only 4 chart pairs (8 total instances), which represents an extremely limited sample size to draw broad conclusions about model consistency.

Experiment 3 evaluates the correction methods on only three mid-sized open-weight models (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, and InternVL2.5-8B), omitting the strongest commercial models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro) which might possess higher table extraction accuracy and potentially benefit differently from redrawing or table-based QA.

Some correction pipelines rely on strong heuristics or prior assumptions, such as knowing the chart type in advance or having access to ground-truth misleader warnings, which somewhat limits immediate end-to-end applicability in unconstrained settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly practical vulnerability in multimodal LLMs (MLLMs): susceptibility to deceptive chart design and misleading visual representations.

Comprehensive empirical investigation evaluating 18 different MLLMs (both state-of-the-art proprietary models and open-weight models of various scales and domain specializations) across 17 misleader types.
Evaluates not only factual QA accuracy (Experiment 1) but also semantic consistency under visual distortions using paired Likert-scale questions (Experiment 2).

Explores six practical inference-time mitigation strategies and provides valuable insights into the fundamental trade-off: eliminating visual distortion via table extraction or chart redrawing helps misleading cases but can penalize clean visualizations due to imperfect intermediate extraction.
weaknesses: The evaluation sample size is relatively modest: the misleading dataset contains 143 instances across 17 categories, meaning several categories have very few samples (e.g., n=1 to 5), limiting the statistical reliability of fine-grained per-misleader claims.
Experiment 2 (consistency evaluation) is based on only four visualization pairs (eight instances in total), which is insufficient to draw broad conclusions about model consistency across chart types.

The mitigation experiments (Experiment 3) are restricted to three open-weight 7B–9B models; testing mitigation on larger frontier models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, InternVL2.5-38B) would substantiate whether the trade-offs observed persist as vision-language extraction capabilities scale.

The correction pipeline relies on heuristic assumptions, such as prior knowledge of chart types for axes/redrawing prompts, without investigating end-to-end automated classification or adaptive invocation of the correction methods.

strengths: Timely and highly relevant topic: As MLLMs are increasingly deployed to extract insights from charts and multimodal data, understanding their susceptibility to deceptive visual tactics (misleaders) is vital for safety, disinformation resistance, and trustworthiness.

Broad and systematic model coverage: The study benchmarks 18 different MLLMs across diverse parameter scales (from 2B to 38B, including specialized chart models and leading frontier closed models like GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro) across 17 distinct misleader categories.

Constructive exploration of mitigation methods: The paper does not merely document failure modes; it implements and systematically tests six inference-time remediation strategies, offering practical insights into trade-offs (e.g., table-based QA vs. redrawing visualization) and highlighting the central role of intermediate table extraction.

Methodological rigor: The study utilizes appropriate statistical validation (e.g., paired t-tests for Likert consistency in Experiment 2, McNemar's tests for accuracy shifts in Experiment 3) and clearly distinguishes between performance on synthetic vs. real-world misleading samples.
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale and skewed distribution: The core evaluation relies on a relatively modest test set of 143 misleading charts across 17 misleader types, resulting in very low sample sizes for several categories (several types have n <= 5, and three have n = 1), which limits the statistical reliability of fine-grained per-category conclusions.

Restricted model scope for correction methods: While 18 models are evaluated in Experiment 1, the mitigation methods in Experiment 3 are only evaluated on three mid-sized open-weight models (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, and InternVL2.5-8B). Evaluating stronger closed models (e.g., GPT-4o) or domain-specific models (e.g., ChartGemma) would provide deeper insight into whether higher-quality table extraction alleviates the performance drop on non-misleading charts.

Lack of direct quantitative evaluation of table extraction: Because table extraction is identified as the key bottleneck for both redrawing and table-based QA, the paper would be significantly strengthened by an explicit, quantitative evaluation of table extraction accuracy (e.g., cell-level precision/recall or normalized tree edit distance) on a subset with ground-truth tables.

Reliance on oracle chart-type metadata: The prompt engineering for axis extraction and chart redrawing assumes prior knowledge of the chart type (e.g., bar, line), which partially idealizes the end-to-end automation pipeline.

strengths: Timely and significant problem formulation: Evaluating whether MLLMs are susceptible to deceptive visual representations addresses a critical gap in automated chart reasoning and multimodal safety.

Extensive model evaluation: The authors systematically evaluate 19 different MLLMs across diverse model families (both closed-source proprietary APIs like GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5, and open-weight models including Qwen2-VL, InternVL2.5, Ovis, etc.), providing a comprehensive state-of-the-art snapshot.

Rigorous mitigation exploration: The paper tests six concrete inference-time mitigation techniques rather than merely diagnosing the failure mode, showing that table-based QA and chart redrawing are effective approaches while simple text warnings fail.

In-depth qualitative and statistical analysis: The paper applies proper significance testing (McNemar's test, paired t-tests) and provides detailed analyses on parametric knowledge leakage, extraction consistency across modalities, and per-misleader breakdowns.
weaknesses: Limited dataset size: The primary evaluation set is modest (n = 143 misleading charts and n = 124 non-misleading charts), with several misleader categories containing very few instances (e.g., n = 1 for overplotting and missing data), limiting the statistical power of granular per-category breakdowns.

Prerequisite assumptions for mitigation: Several mitigation techniques (redrawing and axis extraction) assume prior knowledge of the chart type (e.g., bar, line, pie), and the redrawing approach currently cannot generalize to complex visual elements such as maps or dense scatter plots.

Scope of mitigation testing: While 19 models are evaluated on base vulnerability, Experiment 3 evaluates the correction methods on only three open-weight 7B-9B models, leaving open how closed frontier models respond to these workflows.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely vulnerability in multimodal chart reasoning, demonstrating that state-of-the-art MLLMs degrade almost to random baseline when confronted with misleading visual distortions.
Extensive empirical coverage evaluating 19 open and closed-source MLLMs across 17 misleader types, combining both synthetic benchmarks and newly curated real-world deceptive charts.
Complementary evaluation methodology incorporating both factual QA accuracy and Likert-scale perceptual consistency tests.
Systematic comparison of six inference-time mitigation strategies, highlighting the trade-off between gains on misleading charts and regression on clean/non-misleading charts.
Thorough error analysis and qualitative breakdown detailing how specific visual distortions impede intermediate table and axis extraction.
weaknesses: The evaluation set size for misleading visualizations is relatively small (n = 143 total across 17 categories), meaning several misleader categories contain very few samples (e.g., n <= 3), limiting statistical robustness for fine-grained per-category claims.

The mitigation strategies are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight models (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, InternVL2.5-8B) with a single text LLM (Qwen2.5-7B); exploring whether top-tier commercial models (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude-3.5) similarly benefit from or struggle with table extraction and redrawing would strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

The redrawing and axis-extraction pipelines depend on prior knowledge of the chart type and suffer sharp degradations on non-standard or visually complex charts (such as maps, dual-axis charts, and 3D visual encodings).

strengths: Addresses an important, timely, and underexplored safety/robustness challenge in multimodal NLP: evaluating whether MLLMs are vulnerable to misleading chart designs and visual manipulation.

Comprehensive benchmarking across 19 diverse MLLMs, encompassing leading closed-source frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro), general open-weight models across parameter scales, and chart-specialized models.

Sound evaluation framework that incorporates both objective QA accuracy and cross-visualization consistency (Likert-scale paired tests), as well as a careful investigation into the confounding role of parametric world knowledge.

Systematic comparison of six inference-time mitigation techniques, demonstrating that data derendering (table extraction and redrawing) substantially outperforms prompt warnings and axes injection, while transparently analyzing the trade-off on non-misleading visualizations.

High standard of analysis and reproducibility, featuring detailed per-misleader breakdowns, statistical significance testing (McNemar and paired t-tests), and manual error analyses of intermediate extraction steps in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core evaluation set for misleading visualizations is relatively small (n = 143 across 17 categories), leading to high class imbalance where several misleader categories have very few instances (e.g., n = 1 for overplotting and inappropriate pie charts), limiting the statistical reliability of per-category findings.

The mitigation experiments in Section 3.3 are only evaluated on three mid-sized open-weight models (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, InternVL2.5-8B); evaluating the proposed inference-time defenses on top frontier models (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) would clarify whether these findings generalize to state-of-the-art systems.

The redrawing and axes extraction pipelines assume prior oracle knowledge of the chart type (e.g., bar, line, pie), which simplifies the problem and omits the compounding error of automated chart classification in practical deployments.
